113.title: Watching change
113.hook: steps thirteen to sixteen: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go
113.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, the final steps turn attention to impermanence, the fading of attachment, ending and letting go, and many teachers use the breath's endings as the doorway.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gladdening the mind: known, gladdened, steadied, set free. Your line was release. Did you loosen a grip today? Day one hundred and thirteen, and the last four steps.

Try something. Listen to the next sound you hear. A car, a fridge, a bird. Listen until it stops. Notice the exact moment it ends. Strange, isn't it? We spend almost all our attention on things starting: the new message, the next episode, the plan for tomorrow. Almost none on things ending. But everything ends. Every sound, every mood, every breath. The last four steps of the breathing discourse turn the whole practice toward that plain fact, and they say it's where freedom is found.
screen: `LISTEN UNTIL THE SOUND STOPS.` → `WE WATCH THINGS START.` → `EVERYTHING ENDS.`

segments.voice: The fourth group of four is about seeing things as they really are. Step thirteen: contemplating impermanence, anicca, I will breathe in and out. Step fourteen: contemplating fading away. Step fifteen: contemplating ceasing. Step sixteen: contemplating letting go, relinquishment. Four words, and each goes a little deeper. Impermanence is the plain observation: this breath is changing. It started, it's moving, it's ending. Fading is seeing that as things change, the pull they have on us can fade too. Ceasing is watching things actually end: the breath, the sound, the thought, gone. And letting go is the hand opening, not because you're forced to but because there's nothing left to cling to. The breath is the perfect teacher for this, because it never stops demonstrating. No in-breath lasts. No out-breath can be kept. You can't save a breath for later. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in four words: "All created things perish." It goes on to say that whoever sees this clearly grows weary of pain, and that this is the way to purity. That sounds bleak to some ears. But practitioners describe the opposite. When you really see that everything changes, you stop gripping so hard, and something relaxes. The bad day will end. The good day will end too, which is a reason to taste it while it's here. And every breath becomes both a beginning and an ending. This is where the discourse's sixteen steps arrive: they start with a long breath and end with letting go, and the discourse says breathing practiced this way, all the way through, brings clear knowing and release.
screen: `IMPERMANENCE: THIS BREATH IS CHANGING.` · `FADING: THE PULL FADES TOO.` · `CEASING: WATCH IT END.` · `LETTING GO: THE HAND OPENS.` · then, large: `LET GO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath. Now put your attention on the endings. Notice where each in-breath ends, that small turn at the top. Notice where each out-breath ends, the pause at the bottom. Then widen: notice sounds ending, sensations fading, thoughts dissolving. Nothing to do about it. Just watch things finish. On each out-breath, let something go: a bit of tension, a thought, the need to hold on. The bell holds the time.
Watching change. The last four steps: impermanence, fading, ceasing, and letting go.
Your line: let go. Today, notice one ending: the last sip of coffee, a song finishing, a conversation closing. Let it go. Day one hundred and thirteen.

practitioners describe the opposite: when you stop gripping, something relaxes.
the Dhammapada says all created things perish
Max Müller's translation, verse 277.
you can save a breath for later

options: ignore it: only the breath matters.
notice the ending, and let it go.
wish the sound would come back.
fork.reveal: steps thirteen to sixteen turn attention to change and ending: every ending is a chance to let go.

original.note: Pali: impermanent; Sanskrit anitya. The first of the three marks of existence.

trapdoor: what you thought: nothing lasts, so why bother.
what it means: seeing change, fading, ending and letting go loosens the grip, and something relaxes.
what a scholar hears: steps thirteen to sixteen form the dhammanupassana tetrad of MN 118: anicca, viraga, nirodha, patinissagga; viraga literally means fading of color, and also dispassion.

114.title: Counting
114.hook: an old method: count breaths from one to ten, then begin again
114.howItsDone: Counting breaths from one to ten is taught to beginners in many Buddhist traditions, including Theravada, Zen and Tibetan schools, with the instruction to begin again at one whenever the count is lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, watching change: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go. Your line was let go. What ending did you notice? Day one hundred and fourteen.

Here's a confession almost every meditator makes sooner or later. You sit down to watch the breath. Three breaths in, you're planning dinner. Then you're rehearsing an argument. Then you're wondering if you left the stove on. Five minutes later you remember: oh, right, the breath. Sixteen beautiful steps are no use if you can't stay for two. So the old teachers gave beginners something simpler to hold on to. Something any child can do. They count.
screen: `THREE BREATHS, THEN DINNER PLANS.` → `OH, RIGHT, THE BREATH.` → `SOMETHING SIMPLER: COUNT.`

segments.voice: The method is described in the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, as the very first stage of breath meditation for a beginner: ganana, counting. Breathe in, breathe out: one. Breathe in, breathe out: two. Up to ten. Then back to one. And if you lose count, which you will, you also go back to one. The manual is oddly specific about the numbers. Don't stop below five, it says, and don't go beyond ten. Why? If you only count to three or four, the mind feels cramped and restless, like cattle shut in a pen that's too small. If you count past ten, the mind starts paying attention to the numbers instead of the breath. Five to ten is the sweet spot: long enough to settle, short enough to stay with. The manual also says that once the mind can stay with the breath without the counting, you let the counting go. It's scaffolding, not the building. Counting isn't only a Theravada tool. Zen teachers in Japan and elsewhere also teach beginners to count breaths, often to ten, and many Tibetan teachers use counting too. Here's the part that matters most. Losing count isn't failure. It's the practice. Every time you notice you've drifted off to dinner plans and go back to one, that noticing is the muscle getting stronger. Some people get to ten on their first try. Most don't. Many experienced meditators still don't, on a busy day. And every time, the instruction is the same, with no scolding at all. Back to one.
screen: `ONE TO TEN, THEN BEGIN AGAIN.` · `NOT BELOW FIVE, NOT PAST TEN.` · `SCAFFOLDING, NOT THE BUILDING.` · `LOSING COUNT IS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `BACK TO ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be natural. After each out-breath, count silently: one. Next out-breath: two. Continue to ten, then begin again at one. If you lose track, or catch yourself at fourteen, just smile, and go back to one. No judgment. Try for three rounds, if the time allows; if you only reach three, that's fine too. The counting is a handrail. Keep one hand on it. The bell holds the time.
Counting. An old method for a wandering mind: count breaths from one to ten, and begin again.
Your line: back to one. Today, whenever you lose your place, in a task, a conversation, a plan, say it kindly to yourself: back to one. Day one hundred and fourteen.

what it means: a handrail for a wandering mind, dropped once the mind can stay with the breath.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga VIII lists eight stages of breath practice, beginning with ganana (counting) and anubandhana (connection, following the breath).

115.title: The hindrances arrive
115.hook: desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt: five visitors every sitter meets
115.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators learn to recognize the five hindrances when they arise, noting their presence or absence, as the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness describes, before applying any remedy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, counting: one to ten, and back to one. Your line was back to one. How many times did you go back to one today? Day one hundred and fifteen.

By now you've sat with the breath for a couple of weeks, and you've probably met some visitors. The sudden craving for something sweet. A flash of irritation at the neighbor's music. A heavy, sleepy fog. A restless itch to get up and check something. And that quiet voice asking: is this even working? If you've met all five, congratulations. You're completely normal. The Buddha named these visitors twenty-five centuries ago, and every person who has ever sat down to meditate has met them.
screen: `A CRAVING. A FLASH OF IRRITATION.` → `FOG. ITCH. IS THIS WORKING?` → `FIVE VISITORS, COMPLETELY NORMAL.`

segments.voice: Today's word is nivarana, a hindrance, literally a covering, something that blocks the view. The Pali texts list five. One: sensual desire, wanting pleasant things. Two: ill will, irritation, aversion. Three: sloth and torpor, the heavy, dull, sleepy mind. Four: restlessness and worry, the buzzing mind that can't settle, and the nagging regret. Five: doubt, the wobbling mind that can't commit. In a discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture for each, using a bowl of water that you're trying to see your face in. Desire is water mixed with dye: everything gets tinted. Ill will is water boiling. Dullness is water covered in moss. Restlessness is water whipped up by the wind. Doubt is muddy water set in the dark. In every case, you can't see your reflection clearly. And notice: the water itself is fine. It's what's in it, for now. The first thing the tradition teaches about the hindrances is simply to recognize them. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, when sensual desire is present, the meditator knows: sensual desire is present. When it's absent, they know it's absent. That's it. Before any remedy, you name it. Why does that help? Because a visitor you've named is no longer running the house. Restlessness you've noticed is just restlessness. Restlessness you haven't noticed becomes you, getting up to check your phone. So think of the hindrances as visitors, not enemies. They knock, they come in, they eventually leave. Your job is to see who's here. Name the visitor.
screen: `NIVARANA: A COVERING.` · `FIVE VISITORS, FROM DESIRE TO DOUBT.` · `DYED, BOILING, MOSSY, WINDY, MUDDY.` · `FIRST, JUST NAME IT.` · then, large: `NAME THE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath. As you sit, watch for visitors. When the mind wanders, before coming back, ask: which one is this? Wanting? Irritation? Dullness? Restlessness? Doubt? Name it softly: ah, restlessness. Then return to the breath. If no visitor is present, notice that too: no restlessness now. Don't fight them, and don't feed them. Just see who's here, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Nivarana. A hindrance, a covering: the five visitors every sitter meets.
Your line: name the visitor. Today, when you feel a craving, irritation, fog, restlessness or doubt, name it silently, before you act. Day one hundred and fifteen.

pairs: water whipped up by the wind

every sitter meets them. the Buddha named them because they're normal.
nivarana literally means a covering
something that blocks the view, like dye or mud in water.

fork.setup: you're sitting, and a strong itch to get up and check your phone arrives. what does the discourse say to do first?
fork.reveal: the first step is to recognize it: when restlessness is present, the meditator knows it's present.

original.note: Pali: a hindrance, a covering that blocks the view.

116.title: Your sitting
116.hook: bell, posture, breath, a closing wish of metta
116.howItsDone: Many Buddhists keep a daily sitting practice: a bell or clear start, an upright posture, a breath practice, and a closing wish of loving-kindness or dedication of merit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nivarana: the five hindrances, visitors every sitter meets. Your line was name the visitor. Which one knocked most often? Day one hundred and sixteen, the last day with the breath.

For twenty days you've learned pieces. The four phrases. The sixteen steps. Counting. The visitors. Today we put them together into one thing you can actually do tomorrow morning, and the morning after, without this app, without a teacher, without anything but a place to sit. Many Buddhists have something like this: a simple, repeatable sitting, ten minutes or twenty, done most days. Not a performance. Not a test. Just a habit with a shape to it. Today, you build yours.
screen: `TWENTY DAYS OF PIECES.` → `PUT THEM TOGETHER.` → `A HABIT WITH A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's a simple shape, drawn from what the texts and many teachers describe. First, a bell, or any clear beginning. In many monasteries a bell or gong opens the sitting; it marks the line between the rest of your day and this. A phone timer works fine. Second, posture. The breathing discourse says: sit down, fold the legs crosswise, set the body upright. That's the old ideal, but chairs and cushions both work. What matters is upright without stiffness: a straight back, relaxed shoulders, hands resting, eyes closed or softly lowered. Third, the breath. Use whatever you've learned. Count to ten if the mind is busy. Know the long and the short. Feel the whole body. When a visitor comes, name it, and come back. Don't try all sixteen steps at once. Pick one, and stay with it. Fourth, close with a wish of metta. Before you open your eyes, offer the phrases: to yourself, to someone you love, to everyone. May all beings be at ease. Many Buddhists end their practice this way, sharing whatever good came of the sitting outward. Then the bell again, and back to your day. How long? Ten minutes is a real sitting. Most teachers would rather see ten minutes every day than an hour once a month. And look at the ten days behind you: sixteen steps, long and short, the whole body, joy and ease, the weather of the mind, gladdening, change, counting, the visitors, and now your own sitting. Ten minutes, yours.
screen: `A BELL: THE LINE BETWEEN.` · `UPRIGHT, NOT STIFF.` · `ONE STEP OF THE BREATH.` · `CLOSE WITH METTA.` · then, large: `TEN MINUTES, YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let's walk through it, shorter. The bell has just rung: that's your beginning. Now set your posture: upright, shoulders soft, hands resting. Take one step of the breath, whichever you like best: counting, long and short, or the whole body. Stay with it. When a visitor comes, name it, and return. Near the end, offer the phrases: may I be at ease, may all beings be at ease. Later today, if you can, try the full ten minutes. The bell holds the time.
Your sitting. Bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish of metta: a practice you can keep.
Your line: ten minutes, yours. Today or tomorrow morning, set a timer for ten minutes and do your sitting, start to finish. Day one hundred and sixteen.

117.title: The lane
117.hook: monks walk a straight path of twenty or thirty paces, back and forth
117.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and nuns practice walking meditation on a straight path, often twenty to thirty paces long, walking slowly back and forth, sometimes alternating with sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your sitting: bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish. Your line was ten minutes, yours. Did you get your ten minutes? Day one hundred and seventeen, and the practice stands up.

Think about how you usually walk. To the car. To the kitchen. To the meeting you're late for. Walking is almost always about the destination. The walk itself is dead time between here and there, filled with a phone or a podcast. Now picture a forest monastery in Thailand at dusk. Between the trees there's a narrow, swept path of sand, maybe twenty or thirty steps long. A monk walks slowly to the end, stops, turns, and walks back. And again. And again. For an hour. He's not going anywhere. That's the point.
screen: `WALKING IS ABOUT THE DESTINATION.` → `A SWEPT PATH BETWEEN THE TREES.` → `GOING NOWHERE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is cankama: the walking path, and the practice of walking up and down on it. It's old. In the Pali texts, the Buddha is often found walking up and down in the open air, sometimes late into the night, and monks go to find him on his walking path. The monastic rules describe walking paths and even covered walking halls, so monks could practice in the rain. At Bodh Gaya, tradition marks a spot where the Buddha is said to have walked back and forth in the weeks after his awakening. Why a straight lane, and why so short? Because a lane removes the destination. On a real walk, the mind is always leaning ahead: the corner, the car, the next thing. On a lane of twenty or thirty paces, there's nothing ahead but the end of the lane, and then you turn around. There's nowhere to get to. The mind, with no errand, can finally settle into the walking itself. The feel of the foot. The shift of weight. The ground. Walking meditation is sometimes treated as the lesser cousin of sitting, but many teachers value it highly. It's easier when you're sleepy. It helps when the body is restless. And it's a bridge: you can't sit cross-legged in a grocery store, but you can walk with attention anywhere. Forest monks in Thailand and Sri Lanka may walk for hours a day. Teachers in Burma often alternate an hour of sitting with an hour of walking. For the next six days, you'll learn to walk like this. Today, just the lane. Nowhere to get to.
screen: `CANKAMA: THE WALKING PATH.` · `THE BUDDHA WALKING UP AND DOWN.` · `A LANE REMOVES THE DESTINATION.` · `A BRIDGE TO EVERYDAY LIFE.` · then, large: `NOWHERE TO GET TO.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up. Find a stretch of floor, even just a few paces: a hallway, a quiet corner. Stand at one end, feel your feet on the ground, and let your hands rest in front or behind you. Walk slowly to the other end. Stop. Stand for a breath. Turn. Walk back. Keep your eyes lowered a few steps ahead. When the mind runs off, feel the next step. If you can't stand, feel your feet on the floor from your chair. The bell holds the time.
Cankama. The walking path, and the practice of walking back and forth on it with attention.
Your line: nowhere to get to. Today, find fifteen steps of floor, and walk them slowly there and back, just once. Day one hundred and seventeen.

walking meditation can help when you're sleepy

original.note: Pali: the walking path, and walking up and down on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slow stroll.
what it means: walking with no destination, so the mind can settle into the walking itself.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's Cullavagga permits walking paths and walking halls, and the Ratanacankama shrine at Bodh Gaya marks the walk tradition places in the weeks after the awakening.

118.title: Lifting, moving, placing
118.hook: three parts of a step, named softly
118.howItsDone: In the Burmese noting tradition of Mahasi Sayadaw, meditators walk slowly, silently labeling each part of the step, lifting, moving, placing; other traditions walk with attention but without labels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cankama: the lane, twenty or thirty paces, back and forth. Your line was nowhere to get to. Did you walk your fifteen steps? Day one hundred and eighteen.

You've taken maybe a hundred million steps in your life. Quick question: when your foot leaves the ground, which part leaves first? The heel or the toes? When it comes down, which part lands first? Most people have to stand up and check. We've done it so many times we've stopped feeling it at all. A step has become one blurry thing: walk. Today's practice slows that blur down until you can see the parts inside it. And it gives each part a name.
screen: `A HUNDRED MILLION STEPS.` → `HEEL OR TOES FIRST?` → `SLOW THE BLUR DOWN.`

segments.voice: The method most people learn today comes from Burma, from the twentieth-century teacher Mahasi Sayadaw and his students. Their walking practice uses soft mental labels, called noting. At first, you note just: left, right. Then, as attention sharpens, you break each step into parts. Lifting: the heel rises, the foot comes up. Moving: the foot swings forward through the air. Placing: the foot comes down and touches the ground. Lift, move, place. You say the words silently, lightly, at the same moment as the movement. Not before, not after. The labels are like a flashlight. They keep attention pointed at exactly what's happening. And here's what people discover when they slow down this much: a step is not one thing. Lifting has its own feel, a lightness. Moving has a floating quality. Placing has the pressure, the contact, the weight coming back. Each part begins and ends. That's the same insight you met in the breath, impermanence, now in your feet. The idea of taking a step apart isn't new. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual from the fifth century, analyzes a single step into six parts, from lifting through to pressing down, and says each part arises and passes away in its own moment. Mahasi's three labels are a simpler doorway into the same observation. Some teachers use noting; others, in the Thai forest tradition for instance, simply feel the steps without words, or use a quiet word like Buddho. Different schools, the same attention. And it's slow. Much slower than feels normal. That's fine. Lift, move, place.
screen: `MAHASI SAYADAW'S NOTING.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `A STEP IS NOT ONE THING.` · `SIX PARTS IN THE OLD MANUAL.` · then, large: `LIFT, MOVE, PLACE.`

segments.voice: Stand at one end of your lane, or any few paces of floor. Feel the weight in both feet. Now, very slowly, begin. As the heel rises, silently: lifting. As the foot travels forward: moving. As it touches down: placing. Then the other foot. Let the words be soft, just a whisper in the mind, matching the movement exactly. If the mind wanders, stop, stand, feel the feet, and begin again. If you can't stand, lift and place one foot while seated. The bell holds the time.
Lifting. The first of three parts of a step, named softly: lifting, moving, placing.
Your line: lift, move, place. Today, for ten steps anywhere, the stairs, the hallway, name each part of the step. Day one hundred and eighteen.

match.prompt: the parts of a step — tap the pairs.
pairs: the heel rises, the foot comes up

the old manual breaks a single step into six parts
the Visuddhimagga analyzes a step from lifting through to pressing down.
every Buddhist school uses spoken labels while walking

trapdoor: what you thought: walk slowly.

119.title: The turn
119.hook: the turn at the end of the lane is its own practice
119.howItsDone: In walking meditation, many Buddhists pause at the end of the lane, note standing and the intention to turn, and turn slowly with full attention before walking back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lifting: a step taken apart and named softly. Your line was lift, move, place. Which part of the step surprised you? Day one hundred and nineteen, the end of the week.

Think about the in-between moments of your day. Walking from the car to the door. Waiting for the kettle. The half-second between finishing one email and opening the next. We treat these as nothing, gaps between the real things. And that's exactly where attention leaks away. On the walking lane, the in-between moment is the turn. You reach the end, and there's a little gap before you walk back. Most beginners rush it. Swing around, done. But teachers keep saying the same surprising thing: the turn is its own practice.
screen: `THE IN-BETWEEN MOMENTS.` → `WHERE ATTENTION LEAKS AWAY.` → `THE TURN IS ITS OWN PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: In the Burmese noting method, the turn has its own labels. You reach the end of the lane. Standing, standing: you stop and feel the whole body upright. Then something most people have never noticed: intending to turn. Before the body moves, there's an intention, a tiny decision. The practice asks you to catch it. Then: turning, turning, as the body slowly rotates, one foot at a time. Then standing again. Then intending to walk. And off you go. Why so much fuss about a turn? Because it's where the mind likes to wake up and wander off. Walking in a straight line, attention can settle into a rhythm. At the turn, the rhythm breaks, and the mind jumps to the next thing. If you can stay present through the turn, you can stay present through the bigger turns of the day: getting up, sitting down, walking into a room, starting a new task. And catching the intention matters in Buddhist teaching generally. Intention, cetana, is what the Buddha pointed to as the heart of action. Noticing the small intention before a turn is practice for noticing the bigger ones before you speak or act. Look back at this week too: watching change, counting, the visitors, your own sitting, the lane, the parts of a step, and now the turn. The breath came to your feet. Seven days that moved the practice from the cushion into the body walking. The turn counts too, and so do all the in-between moments.
screen: `STANDING, STANDING.` · `INTENDING TO TURN.` · `TURNING, TURNING.` · `THE BIGGER TURNS OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE TURN COUNTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Stand at one end of your few paces of floor. Walk slowly to the other end. Now stop, and feel yourself standing. Notice the wish to turn, before you move. Then turn slowly, one small step at a time, feeling the feet shift and the body rotate. Stand again for a breath. Notice the wish to walk. Then walk back. Let each turn be as careful as each step. If you're seated, practice turning your head slowly, noticing the intention first. The bell holds the time.
The turn. The moment at the end of the lane: standing, intending, turning, a practice of its own.
Your line: the turn counts too. Today, catch one in-between moment, standing up, opening a door, and notice the intention before you move. Day one hundred and nineteen.

match.prompt: the parts of the turn — tap the pairs.
pairs: stop and feel the body upright

myth: the turn is just a break between the real walking
teachers call it its own practice: it's where the mind likes to wander.
there's an intention before the body turns
the practice asks you to catch it: intending to turn.
the Buddha pointed to intention as the heart of action
cetana: what you intend is what shapes the act.

fork.setup: you reach the end of your walking lane. what do you do?
options: swing around quickly and keep going.
stop, notice the intention, and turn slowly.
fork.reveal: standing, intending to turn, turning: the turn gets the same attention as every step.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: intention, volition; the Buddha calls it the heart of action.

trapdoor: what you thought: the turn is how you get back.
what it means: a moment to stay present through a change, and to catch the intention before you move.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.63 has the Buddha say that intention is what he calls kamma; the turning labels come from the Mahasi noting method.

sources.ref: AN 6.63, Nibbedhika Sutta: intention is kamma
